title: Underwater neutrino detector sets new limits on Einstein's special relativity
excerpt: KM3NeT collaboration finds no violation of Lorentz invariance – yet
content:
Measurements of neutrino oscillations have placed new constraints on possible violations of Lorentz invariance – a fundamental principle of special relativity. The measurements were made using the KM3NeT collaboration’s partially completed undersea neutrino telescopes, and although the data show no signs of invariance violations, collaboration members say it is encouraging that their 18-month observing run delivered results on par with 12 years of observations from Japan’s Super-Kamiokande neutrino detector.

“One of these constraints is also comparable to the result obtained by the neutrino detector IceCube using two years of data,” adds study co-leader Alba Domi, an astroparticle physicist at FAU Erlangen-Nürnberg in Germany. “And we have established the first direct constraints on additional new parameters – including those on possible differences in the behaviour of two types, or flavours, of neutrinos, the muon and tau neutrinos.”

General relativity vs quantum field theory

One of the biggest open questions in physics is how to reconcile general relativity, which describes gravity and the universe at large scales, and quantum field theory, which explains the behaviour of particles at the smallest scales. Although both theories are remarkably successful, they are mutually inconsistent, meaning that we do not yet have a unified theory of quantum gravity.

One possible route to developing such a theory is to study how gravity affects quantum objects. Although any such effects would be extremely small and hard to observe directly, some theoretical approaches suggest they could manifest in tiny deviations from standard predictions. Violations of Lorentz invariance are a particularly interesting possibility. Named after the Dutch physicist Hendrik Lorentz, and incorporated into Albert Einstein’s theory of special relativity in 1905, the principle of Lorentz invariance states that the laws of physics should be the same for all inertial observers everywhere in the universe – that is, physics should work the same for anyone moving at a steady speed, wherever they are.

 Because neutrinos can travel huge distances, are observed across an enormous range of energies, and oscillate between different flavours as they propagate, even very small deviations from Lorentz invariance could leave observable signatures in their energy and the direction in which they propagate. For these reasons, Domi says, studying neutrinos is a promising way of searching for these deviations.

A new neutrino telescope beneath the Mediterranean Sea

Among the newest facilities for such neutrino studies is KM3NeT, which consists of two underwater neutrino telescopes that use highly sensitive light detectors to register the faint flashes of light produced when neutrinos interact with matter. The first telescope, ORCA (Oscillation Research with Cosmics in the Abyss) is located about 40 km off the coast of Toulon, France, at a depth of approximately 2450 m. It detects neutrinos with relatively low energies (from a few GeV to several TeV) that are produced in the Earth’s atmosphere, and is geared to measure how these neutrinos oscillate between different flavours.

The second telescope, ARCA (Astroparticle Research with Cosmics in the Abyss) is located at a depth of roughly 3500 m off the Portopalo di Capo Passero on the Sicilian coast. As well as detecting atmospheric neutrinos, it also detects much higher-energy neutrinos arriving from astrophysical sources.

In the new work, which is detailed in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics, the KM3NeT researchers compared the neutrino energies observed at the ORCA detector, and the directions from which they arrived, with parameters predicted by theory. This allowed them to explore a broad range of Lorentz-violating parameters, including some that had never been directly constrained before.

While the neutrino distributions they observed were consistent with the predictions of standard physics, with no evidence of Lorentz invariance violations, this does not mean that such violations are absent. “If such effects exist,” Domi stresses, “they may simply be too small for us to detect with our current dataset.”

The observations do, however, allow researchers to quantify just how small these effects must be, and set upper limits on the strength of possible Lorentz-violating contributions. “These limits help narrow down the range of theoretical models that remain compatible with experimental observations,” Domi explains.

Competing with established experiments

According to the team, the study shows that KM3NeT/ORCA can compete with established experiments even at this early stage of its operation. “Our new result is particularly remarkable considering that we analysed data collected with only the first six units of the ORCA detector,” says Lukas Hennig, a PhD student in Domi’s group. “At term, ORCA, will boast 108 of these and will therefore be able to probe fundamental properties of spacetime with unprecedented sensitivity.”

Since the effects of Lorentz invariance violation on neutrino propagation grow linearly with the distance travelled by a neutrino and depend on its energy, astrophysical neutrinos – ARCA’s speciality – make particularly powerful probes for tiny deviations. With both ORCA and ARCA still moving towards their final configurations, however, Domi says the team’s immediate focus will be to analyse atmospheric neutrinos detected by ORCA and ARCA. “The increasing statistics we obtain will allow us to further improve our constraints,” she tells Physics World.
